title: Landfall
short: Welcome to Rhodes. Before you walk, stand still for a moment at the bottom of the gangway and look west, at the wall. For three thousand years people have arrived on this shore the way you just did: from the water, looking at the town. Greeks. Romans. Byzantines. Crusaders. Ottomans. Italians. You. Some came to trade. Some came to take it. The city in front of you was built around a single certainty: that someone was always coming. Everything you see today, the moat, the bastions, the gates, is an answer to that. The nearest gate is to your right, about five minutes along the quay. Walk toward the wall, and keep the sea on your left.
long:
Welcome to Rhodes. Before you walk, stand still for a moment at the bottom of the gangway and look west, toward the wall. For three thousand years people have arrived on this shore the way you just did: from the water, looking at the town. Greeks first, in three cities, then one. Romans, who came here to learn how to speak. Byzantines. Crusaders. Ottomans. Italians. And now you, off a ship the size of a small town. Some came to trade. Some came to take it. Some came because they had nowhere else to go.

The harbour you are standing in has a name for that. In the year three hundred and five before Christ, a Macedonian prince called Demetrius, later nicknamed the Besieger, sailed into this bay with two hundred warships and more than a hundred and seventy transports, forty thousand men, and behind them almost a thousand private ships full of traders hoping to pick over the wreckage. He floated a boom of spiked logs across the entrance. The Rhodians answered with fire ships packed with pitch. You will hear how that ended later, at the harbour mouth, because the ending is a thirty-three metre bronze statue of the sun.

For now, one fact. The city in front of you was designed around a single certainty: that someone was always coming. Everything you will see today, the moat, the bastions, the gates, the round towers, is an answer to that. It is also a city nobody ever abandoned. Everyone who took it kept using it, and so it is not a museum of one moment. It is a stack of centuries, and today we walk down through them and back up again.

The nearest gate is to your right, about five minutes along the quay, a wide opening in the sea wall called the Gate of the Virgin. Walk toward the wall, keep the sea on your left, and do not go through yet. The next track starts at the gate.

One practical note. Another ship arrived at seven this morning, so the Palace and the museum will be busiest from mid-morning. We go there first. Lunch is booked for later. Your ship sails at six, and sunset is at six fifty-four, which means the best light of the day will be from the top deck, with this wall sliding astern. Nobody has to hurry back for it.

title: The Threshold
short: Stop before the arch. Do not go through yet. Turn around, and look at where you came from. Your ship. The water. And, framing it all, medieval stone. This opening was cut in nineteen fifty-five, which makes it the youngest thing in the wall, but the wall itself is what the Knights of Saint John left behind after two hundred years of expecting the worst. Take the picture if you want it. Then turn back to the arch. When you walk through, the twenty-first century stays behind you. Go.
long:
Stop before the arch. Do not go through yet.

Turn around and look at where you came from. Your ship, filling the harbour. The water. The quay you just walked. And framing all of it, on either side of you, stone that was cut for cannon. This is a picture that only exists here, so take it if you want it.

The opening itself is a cheat. The Gate of the Virgin was cut through the sea wall in nineteen fifty-five for traffic, on a plan the Italians drew. The Knights had no gate here. Their harbour gates were the small Mills Gate just to the north, which led out to the grain mills on the mole, and the great twin-towered Marine Gate beyond it, which you will meet in a few minutes. This breach is named for the church just inside it, and that church is the reason we came in this way.

A word about who built the wall you are standing in. The Knights Hospitaller of Saint John began as a hospital in Jerusalem, became a religious order, then a military one, lost the Holy Land, spent a few years on Cyprus, and in thirteen ten took Rhodes from the Byzantines after a four-year siege of their own. For the next two hundred and twelve years this island was their sovereign state, and this town was its capital. They were expelled from here in fifteen twenty-three, and only afterward became the Knights of Malta. So everything you will see of them today is the original: the Malta you may know is the sequel.

They built for siege because sieges came. Four kilometres of wall. A dry moat up to thirty metres wide. Walls twelve metres thick in places. A ring of round bastions added every time a new kind of gun appeared. You will walk on top of those walls at noon.

Now turn back to the arch. When you walk through it, the twenty-first century stays behind you. The lane on the other side leads into the oldest surviving neighbourhood of the town, and the first thing you meet is a church with no roof. Go.

title: A Church Without a Roof
short: On your left, just inside the gate, a church with the sky for a ceiling. Our Lady of the Burgh, fourteenth century, Gothic, three apses still standing against the blue. Step inside the arches if the gate is open. Close your eyes for ten seconds and imagine the roof back on, the choir, the candle smoke, the stone reverb. … Now open them. Wind. Sea. Cats. This is what Rhodes does to buildings. It uses them until they fall down and then it uses the pieces. Christian church, Ottoman town, Allied bombs, a garden of arches. Walk on through the lanes toward the square with the fountain.
long:
On your left, just inside the gate, is a church with the sky for a ceiling. Our Lady of the Burgh, fourteenth century, Gothic, three apses still standing against the blue, the pointed arches of a cathedral nave with nothing on top of them.

Step inside the arches if the gate is open. Stand in what was the nave. Close your eyes for ten seconds and put the roof back on. Choir. Candle smoke. The stone reverb of a cold building full of people. … Now open them. Wind. Sea. A cat. This is what Rhodes does to buildings. It uses them until they fall down, and then it uses the pieces.

The Burgh, the Bourgo, was the lower town, the merchants' town. The Knights lived in their own walled quarter on the hill to the north, the Collachium, and nobody who was not a member of the Order was allowed to sleep there overnight. Everyone else, the Greeks, the Latin traders, the Jews, lived down here, ruled but not admitted. This church was theirs, the Latin church of the lower town, and it was already old when the Knights lost the island.

After fifteen twenty-two the Greeks were moved out of the walls altogether into suburbs, the churches became mosques, and enclosed wooden balconies were hung over these lanes. In the twentieth century the Italians tore the balconies down again to make the town look medieval, which it had never quite been. In nineteen forty-four Allied bombs fell on this quarter. The church lost whatever the centuries had left it. What you are looking at is honest ruin, and it is one of the most beautiful things in the town.

This is also the doorway to the Juderia, the Jewish quarter, which is a five-minute walk south of here. We will come back to it after noon, when the synagogue is open, and we will give it its own quiet track. For now, turn west, away from the sea, and follow the lanes toward the square with the fountain and the stone owl. It is about four minutes. The town wakes up as you go.

title: The Law Is Lord of the Sea
short: You are in Hippocrates Square, the heart of the lower town. The building with the outside staircase is the Castellania, fifteen oh seven, the Knights' courthouse. A stone owl sits on the fountain. Ignore anyone waving a menu at you here; the good tables are one lane away. Under the courthouse stairs, since nineteen sixty-three, a family cellar pours Rhodian wine by the glass. Remember it for later. Now walk the fifty metres to the twin-towered gate facing the harbour. That is the Marine Gate, and it is where Rhodes wrote the law of the sea.
long:
You are in Hippocrates Square, the heart of the lower town, where the bazaar street comes down the hill and the harbour gate opens to the water. The building with the outside stone staircase is the Castellania, built in fifteen oh seven, the Knights' courthouse, where the Order judged the merchants it taxed. A stone owl sits on the fountain. Ignore anyone waving a laminated menu at you on this square. The honest kitchens are one lane away, on a quiet street called Sofokleous, and lunch is already planned there. But note the little doorway under the courthouse stairs. Since nineteen sixty-three a family has run a cellar there that pours Rhodian wine by the glass to drink on the steps, and sells the island's grape spirit, souma, at shop prices. That is a later stop.

Now walk the fifty metres north to the gate with the two round towers facing the harbour. This is the Marine Gate, built by Grand Master Pierre d'Aubusson in fourteen seventy-eight, as much for show as defence: look for the saints carved above the arch. Its north tower was shattered by Allied bombing and rebuilt in nineteen fifty-one. From this quay, on the first of January fifteen twenty-three, the Knights sailed away for good, with drums beating and four thousand townspeople who chose exile with them. You will hear that story on the walls.

Stand under the arch and look at the water, because this gate is the right place for the oldest thing Rhodes gave the world. Not the statue. The law.

Two thousand years ago Rhodes ran the biggest merchant fleet in the eastern Mediterranean, and it wrote rules for it. One survived into Roman law and is still in every marine insurance policy on earth. If cargo is thrown overboard to save a ship, everyone whose goods were saved shares the loss. Lawyers call it general average. The Romans called it the Rhodian law.

There is a story about it in the Digest of Justinian. A merchant named Eudaemon was shipwrecked off an island and robbed by the islanders, and he petitioned the emperor Antoninus. The emperor wrote back: I am, indeed, the Lord of the World. But the Law is the Lord of the sea, and this affair must be decided by the Rhodian law.

Hold on to that. Everything else you will see today is about people trying to take this town by force. This gate is a reminder that for a few centuries Rhodes ruled the water with a rule book.

When you are ready, go back through the gate and follow the lane north along the inside of the wall. In about three minutes it opens into Museum Square, and the great building on your left is the reason the Knights existed at all.

title: The Hospital
short: The building filling the south side of Museum Square is the Hospital of the Knights. Not a castle. A hospital. That is what the Order was for, before it was anything else: they called the sick our lords, and knights of the French tongue nursed them in person in the great ward upstairs, a hall with seven octagonal pillars. Inside now is the Archaeological Museum. Three things to find. The marble head of Helios, drilled for a bronze crown of rays, the closest surviving face to the Colossus. The crouching Aphrodite of Rhodes, wringing out her hair. And the Marine Venus, worn smooth by the sea. Go in now, before the crowds. Give it forty-five minutes.
long:
The building filling the south side of Museum Square, and the whole left-hand side of the street that climbs away from it, is the Hospital of the Knights. Not a castle. A hospital. Begun in fourteen forty on the ruins of a Roman building, finished in fourteen eighty-nine under Grand Master d'Aubusson, whose name you will keep hearing today.

Above the door, two angels hold the arms of Grand Master Fluvian, who left the money. Inside, a courtyard with a stone lion and a heap of stone cannonballs, then a monumental stair to the first floor. The great ward up there is a hall divided by seven octagonal pillars, with a chapel apse at the end, isolation cells along the sides and a cedar ceiling. It held about a hundred patients, tended by the knights themselves.

This matters for everything else you see today. The Order of Saint John began in Jerusalem as a hospice for pilgrims, became a religious order, then a military one, then a sovereign state. But the vow that defined them was to serve, in their own phrase, our lords the sick. The tongue of France, the richest of the eight national chapters, held the office of Hospitaller, master of this house. A young knight who arrived on Rhodes had to serve his turn here and sail three patrols on the Order's galleys before he could hope for a posting home. Warrior monks, yes. But the building they were proudest of was this one.

It is now the Archaeological Museum, and three things inside belong to today's story.

First, the marble head of Helios, the sun god, over life size, second century before Christ. Look at the hair, windswept and drilled with holes. Those held a bronze crown of rays. This is the closest surviving thing to the face of the Colossus, and it was found on the hill at the top of this street, where the Palace now stands. Remember that when we get up there.

Second, the Aphrodite of Rhodes: a small crouching Venus, half a metre high, wringing the sea out of her hair and looking straight at you. Found in nineteen twenty-three in the governor's garden.

Third, the Marine Venus, a standing Aphrodite fished out of the harbour in nineteen twenty-nine, her face worn smooth by the sea. She was hidden in a crypt during the war. In nineteen forty-five the writer Lawrence Durrell, who was living in a gatekeeper's lodge in an Ottoman cemetery on the far side of town, watched her come out. I can still see the faces of my friends, he wrote, as they surrounded the dark trap door out of which she rose so gravely into the sunlight. He named his book about Rhodes after her.

One practical note. Another cruise ship has been in port since seven. Go in now, while the alleys are still quiet. Give it forty-five minutes. The Prehistoric rooms are open today; the Epigraphical rooms are not, so do not hunt for them. When you come out, turn left up the cobbled street. That climb is the next track.

title: Seven Tongues
short: Start walking uphill. This is the Street of the Knights: two hundred metres, six metres wide, the spine of the Knights' private quarter. The Order was run by national chapters called tongues, and each had its inn here. On your right, first: the Inn of Italy, fifteen nineteen. Then the Inn of France, the richest facade on the street. Look up. Crocodiles. Those gargoyles commemorate a dragon, and you will meet it at the top of the hill. Across the street, the Inn of Spain, and joined to it by the arch overhead, the Inn of Provence. Every shield on this street is a signature.
long:
Start walking uphill. Slowly. This is the Street of the Knights, the Odos Ippoton: two hundred metres long, six metres wide, cobbled, rising gently west from the Hospital to the Palace. It is the spine of the Collachium, the walled quarter where only members of the Order could sleep, and it is the most complete medieval street in the eastern Mediterranean. In nineteen sixteen the Italians stripped off the Ottoman wooden balconies to make it look the way it did in fourteen ninety. The stone, the arches and the coats of arms are original.

Here is how the Order worked, because this street is its organisation chart carved in stone. The Knights were divided by nation into chapters called tongues, langues. Provence, Auvergne, France, Italy, Aragon, England and Germany, and after fourteen sixty-two an eighth, Castile. Each tongue lived in its own inn, ate together, and defended its own stretch of the city wall. And the head of each tongue held one of the great offices by right of his nation. Provence gave the Grand Commander, the treasurer. Auvergne gave the Marshal, who commanded the army. France gave the Hospitaller. Italy gave the Admiral. Aragon the standard-bearer. England the Turcopolier, the captain of the light cavalry and the coast watch. Germany the Grand Bailiff, in charge of the walls. Castile the Chancellor. A game designer would be embarrassed to invent it.

Now read the street as you climb. Right-hand side, first building: the Inn of Italy, fifteen nineteen. The shield in the centre of the facade belongs to Grand Master Fabrizio del Carretto, the last Grand Master to die on Rhodes, a year before the final siege.

Next on the right, the Inn of France, the richest facade here, restored around fourteen ninety-two after the first siege. A corner turret. The arms of d'Aubusson with his cardinal's hat. Three plaques of Villiers de l'Isle-Adam, the last Grand Master of Rhodes. And look up at the roofline. Crocodiles. Those gargoyles commemorate the dragon that a Grand Master killed in the fourteenth century, and you will meet it at the top of the hill, at the gate where its skull hung. Four of the last five Grand Masters were Frenchmen, two of them from this house. Chateaubriand admired the lilies of France here, as fresh as if they came from the hand of the sculptor.

Beside the Inn of France, a tiny Gothic chapel, thirteen sixty-five, with the arms of the Pope framed by the lions of England: it began as the English chapel. Then the chaplain's house, with ten shields on its lintel, a who's who of fourteenth-century Grand Masters.

Left-hand side, near the top, the Inn of Spain, one of the largest, with the shields of Castile, Aragon, Granada, Navarre and Portugal, and joined to it by the arch that bridges the street, the Inn of Provence, fifteen eighteen, the oldest tongue and the Grand Commander's seat.

Every shield on this street is a signature. The street ends in a vaulted arcade, the Loggia of Saint John, and opens onto the Palace forecourt. Stop under the arcade. The next track is about what used to stand on your left.

title: The Vault
short: Look left from the top of the street, past the clock tower, to the school building. Under that school lie the foundations of the Church of Saint John, the Order's own church, begun in thirteen ten. Six Grand Masters were buried in it. Its treasury held the right hand of John the Baptist. After the conquest it became the town's main mosque, and somebody stored gunpowder under the bell tower. On the sixth of November eighteen fifty-six, lightning struck. The church vanished. The Palace lost its upper floors. At least two hundred people died. A dungeon trap with a three-hundred-year fuse.
long:
Look left from the top of the street, past the Ottoman clock tower, to the neoclassical school building. Under that school, and only scraps of foundation show beside it, lie the remains of the Church of Saint John of the Collachium, the Order's own church, begun in thirteen ten, a year after they took the island.

This was the heart of the faction. The Grand Masters were crowned here and buried here; at least six of them, including the dragon-slayer Dieudonné de Gozon, whose plain tomb slab was dug up and shipped to Paris in eighteen seventy-seven. It sits today in the Musée de Cluny. And this was the treasury. The relics the Order carried out of the Holy Land were kept here: a fragment of the True Cross, the icon of Our Lady of Philermos credited with saving the city in fourteen eighty, and, attested in this church from fourteen thirteen, the right hand of John the Baptist himself, the hand that baptised Christ.

Follow that hand for a moment, because its journey is the best artifact story on the island. It left Rhodes with the Knights in fifteen twenty-three. It went to Malta. When Napoleon took Malta in seventeen ninety-eight, the Knights handed it to the Tsar of Russia, who dressed the icon in diamonds. When the revolution came, the Dowager Empress carried the relics out through Copenhagen. They went to the King of Yugoslavia in Belgrade, were hidden in a mountain monastery in nineteen forty-one, seized by the communist police in nineteen fifty-one and locked in a vault in Cetinje, Montenegro. Their survival was revealed only in nineteen ninety-three. The hand is in a monastery in Cetinje today. A nine-century game of keep-away, and it started in the ground you are looking at.

After the conquest of fifteen twenty-two the church became the town's main mosque. And at some point, somebody stored gunpowder in the cellars under its bell tower. On the sixth of November eighteen fifty-six, lightning struck the tower. The church vanished in a single blast. The upper floors of the Palace behind you were blown apart. Much of the Knights' quarter came down. At least two hundred people died, and the British vice-consul, an amateur archaeologist named Biliotti, spent days digging for survivors. The clock tower you can see was rebuilt afterward. The Italians, seventy years later, built a copy of the lost church from old engravings down at the harbour, and you will walk past it this afternoon.

If you play games, you already know what this is. A reliquary chapel over a forgotten powder magazine. A trap with a three-hundred-and-thirty-four-year fuse.

Now turn right, to the gate with the two horseshoe towers. That is the Palace of the Grand Master, and the hill it stands on may be the most argued-about piece of ground on the island.

title: The Keep on the Sun's Hill
short: The Palace of the Grand Master. A Byzantine citadel first, the Order's headquarters from thirteen oh nine, wrecked in the explosion, and rebuilt in the nineteen thirties as a holiday residence for the King of Italy and Mussolini, who never came. Upstairs, mosaics lifted from the island of Kos. Downstairs, today, the Ancient Rhodes exhibition, with stone shot from the siege engines that paid for the Colossus. And the hill itself: the best current scholarship says the sanctuary of Helios stood here, and so did the statue. Buy the walls-walk ticket at the desk. Go in about eleven, and at noon go straight to the iron gate.
long:
You are standing in front of the Palace of the Grand Master. Walk through the gate between the two horseshoe towers into the courtyard, and let me tell you what you are actually looking at, because it is not quite what it seems.

The hill was a Byzantine citadel in the seventh century. The Knights made it their headquarters after thirteen oh nine: a fortress roughly eighty metres square around a courtyard, with grain silos along one side for sieges. Then the powder magazine under the church next door went up in eighteen fifty-six, and for eighty years this was a ruin.

What you walk through today was built between nineteen thirty-seven and nineteen forty by the Italian governor of the Dodecanese, as a holiday residence for King Victor Emmanuel the Third and for Mussolini. Neither of them ever slept here. The architect worked from the outside walls inward and invented most of the rest; critics at the time called it horrible fascist taste. The floors upstairs are paved with Hellenistic and Roman mosaics lifted from the island of Kos in the nineteen thirties: the Nine Muses, the Medusa in the colonnaded hall, a nymph on a sea-horse. There is a full-size cast of the Laocoön, the marble group of a priest and his sons strangled by sea serpents, which was carved by three sculptors from Rhodes and is one of the most famous statues in the world. Jewish tombstones from the town cemetery were requisitioned for the building work. So the Palace is a palimpsest of regimes: a Byzantine fort, a crusader keep, an exploded ruin, and a dictator's unused summer house.

Downstairs, and open today, is the exhibition Ancient Rhodes, Two Thousand Four Hundred Years. Look for the stone shot, the great round balls fired from Demetrius' siege engines in three hundred and five BC. That siege is the one that paid for the Colossus, and I will tell it at the harbour this afternoon.

Now the hill itself. For seven hundred years people have argued about where the Colossus stood, and most of them have looked at the harbour. In twenty twenty-four an Oxford monograph by Nathan Badoud, which reviewers are calling the definitive study, argued that the sanctuary of Helios, the sun god's sacred area, was here, on this small hill at the head of the Knights' quarter. An inscription naming the sacred area of Helios, dedications by his priests, and that marble head you saw in the Hospital were all found on this hill. A statue here would have been visible from the Anatolian coast, which Rhodes then ruled. So when you stand in the courtyard, picture a bronze youth a hundred feet tall where the towers are. We will come back to this at the harbour, and the answer will point up here.

Practical. Buy the walls-walk ticket at the desk when you buy the Palace ticket. The rampart walk runs only from noon to three on weekdays, and if you leave the Palace and come back for it you pay the twenty euros again, so go in around eleven and stay. Last admission is twenty minutes before closing. There is one more stop before noon, and it is five minutes away: out through the small gate on the west side of the forecourt, to the great gate beyond it. Bring a look-up.

title: Draconis Extinctor
short: You are under the arch of the d'Amboise Gate, the grandest in the circuit, fifteen twelve. Look up. Local tradition says that a skull hung over this gate until eighteen thirty-seven. The skull of a dragon. Around thirteen forty a beast in a marsh below the hill to the west was eating shepherds, and knights. The Grand Master forbade any further attempt. A young knight named Dieudonné de Gozon went home to France, built a dragon of wood and canvas, trained two dogs on it for months, came back, and killed it. Everyone who saw the head over the gate called it a crocodile.
long:
You are under the arch of the d'Amboise Gate, finished in fifteen twelve by Grand Master Emery d'Amboise, the grandest gate in the whole circuit. A marble angel holds the arms of the Order. There are slots in the twin round towers where the drawbridge chains ran. Behind you the road bends through three more gates before it reaches the town, which is why the Ottomans called it the Crooked Gate: a killing corridor with cannon at ground level.

Now look up at the arch, because local tradition says that until about eighteen thirty-seven a skull hung over this gate, and it was the skull of a dragon.

Here is the story as it has been told since the sixteenth century. Around thirteen forty, under Grand Master Hélion de Villeneuve, a monster made its lair in the marsh and caves at Malpasso, the bad passage, on the coast road a couple of kilometres south-west of here, under the hill they now call Monte Smith. It ate cattle. It ate shepherds. Knights rode out and did not come back. The Grand Master forbade any further attempt, on pain of expulsion.

A young knight from Provence, Dieudonné de Gozon, went home to his father's castle in France. He built a dragon of wood and canvas, hid meat under its belly, and for months trained two mastiffs to dart at the soft underside, and his horse to charge it. Then he came back to Rhodes and rode out with two squires. His lance shattered on the scales. The dogs hung on the belly. He drove his sword into the one place it could go. The dying beast fell on him, and the squires revived him with cold water. Villeneuve stripped him of the habit for disobedience, then, moved by his humility, gave it back. In thirteen forty-six Gozon became Grand Master. His epitaph, the story says, read Draconis Extinctor. Slayer of the dragon. Schiller made a ballad of it in seventeen ninety-eight whose moral was obedience.

Now the historian's cut. In nineteen thirteen a British scholar named Hasluck went looking for the sources. He found nothing before fifteen twenty-one, and in that account the hero has no name. The name Gozon was first attached by Bosio, writing in Rome in the fifteen nineties. A French traveller in the sixteen fifties saw a head over a gate, larger than a horse's, with a huge mouth and teeth and very large eyes, and every later witness who described it said the same thing: crocodile. Some said hippopotamus. Hasluck's explanation is that Gozon had marched in French religious processions where a model dragon, the spirit of evil, was ritually slain, and the parade turned into a biography.

And there is an older layer under that. Pliny lists the island's ancient names and one of them is Ophiussa, the snaky one. Diodorus says Rhodes was once infested with serpents until the oracle of Apollo told the people to summon a Thessalian named Phorbas, who killed them and was honoured as a hero ever after. Rhodes was the snake island before it was the dragon island. Same story, older monster.

So: a quest forbidden by your own order, training on a dummy, a crocodile skull over the city gate. Decide for yourself. Then go back through the three gates the way you came, to the Palace forecourt. The iron gate to the ramparts opens at noon.

title: The Faction Map
short: You are on top of the wall. No railings on the inside; keep to the middle. Walk south. Every stretch of this rampart belonged to one tongue of the Order, and its arms are carved on the stone. First France, then Germany. The pentagonal bastion below you is Saint George, a prototype of every star fort in Europe; the earth bank behind it was honeycombed with tunnels rigged to collapse on anyone who got in. Then Auvergne, then the Tower of Spain, taken and retaken on the twenty-fourth of September fifteen twenty-two. Then the long English curtain, where two mines blew a twelve-yard hole on the fourth of September. The walk ends at the Red Gate.
long:
You are on top of the wall. It is wide enough for two carts, they say, and there are no railings on the inside, so keep to the middle and look where you step. Walk south, with the moat on your right. This is a faction map, and you are walking across it.

The Order divided the circuit among its tongues, and each tongue's arms are carved on its stretch. From the Palace the first post was France. Then Germany, whose Grand Bailiff was responsible for all the fortifications. Below you now is the pentagonal Bastion of Saint George, wrapped around an old gate that d'Aubusson walled shut after the first siege and given its final form by an engineer from Vicenza before the second. Historians call it a prototype of the angled bastion, the shape that would define European fortresses for three hundred years. The earth bank behind it, the terreplein of Spain, was honeycombed with galleries built to be collapsed on any attacker who got inside.

The next post is Auvergne, the Marshal's tongue. And then the Tower of Spain. Here is the first set-piece. Rhodes was besieged twice by the Ottoman Empire. The first time, in fourteen eighty, it held. The second time, in fifteen twenty-two, Sultan Suleiman came in person, with something like a hundred thousand men and four hundred ships, against about seven hundred knights and six thousand soldiers. On the twenty-fourth of September, the day of the great general assault, the Janissaries took this tower by midday and planted their banners on the rampart you are walking on. A knight named Jacques de Bourbon led his brothers back through the underground passages and retook it. It changed hands twice more before Suleiman called off the attack and sentenced his own commander to death, then relented.

Now the long straight stretch ahead of you. This was England's post, between the gate of Saint Athanasios and the gate of Saint John. The Ottomans had brought thousands of miners, and they dug forty or more tunnels under the moat you are looking at. The defenders' answer was a Venetian engineer named Gabriele Tadini, smuggled out of Crete against orders in July. He pressed a drum with bells hung on its skin against the walls of his own galleries, and when the bells rang he knew where the enemy picks were biting. Then he either broke into their tunnel and fought in the dark, or blew it from below. On the fourth of September two mines got through and opened a twelve-yard breach in this wall. The English brothers and the Grand Master in person held it all day. On the fourteenth of October Tadini took an arquebus ball through the eye while looking through a gun slit. Titian later painted him with one eye. Six weeks later he was leading a sortie.

And the treason. The Chancellor of the Order, Andrea d'Amaral, who had lost the election for Grand Master the year before, was accused after his servant was caught on the ramparts with a bow and a letter to shoot into the enemy lines. The servant was hanged and quartered. D'Amaral refused to confess under torture, was stripped of his habit in the church of Saint John and beheaded. Portuguese historians call him a scapegoat. Hold both versions.

By December the powder was gone and the Spanish tower had fallen for good. On the twenty-second the town accepted terms. The Knights could leave with their arms, their relics and their honour; the churches were not to be desecrated; the islanders would pay no tax for five years. Suleiman rode in on Christmas Day. On the first of January fifteen twenty-three, fifty ships sailed from the harbour with drums beating, carrying the Order, four thousand Rhodians who chose to go with it, and a new banner: the Virgin with her dead son, and the motto Afflictis spes mea rebus. In my afflictions, my hope. Seven years later the Emperor gave them Malta.

The last posts are Provence, and then Italy at the harbour corner, where the first siege had broken through in fourteen eighty. You will hear that one from below, at the round bastion. The walk ends at the Gate of Saint John, the Kokkini Porta, the Red Gate, so called, the legend says, because the blood of fifteen twenty-two dyed its stones. Steep concrete steps at the end. The Jewish quarter is five minutes north of where you come down.

title: La Juderia
short: Two streets north of the Red Gate, on Dosiadou street, is Kahal Shalom, fifteen seventy-seven, the oldest synagogue in Greece. Jews have lived on Rhodes for more than two thousand years. By nineteen thirty, four thousand people spoke Ladino in these lanes, in a quarter with six synagogues. On the twenty-third of July nineteen forty-four, one thousand six hundred and seventy-three of them were marched from the square just ahead to the harbour, and put on three boats. About one hundred and fifty came back. Go inside. The museum is in the old women's prayer rooms. Take your time. The track ends here.
long:
Two streets north of the Red Gate, on the corner of Dosiadou and Simiou streets, is Kahal Shalom. Fifteen seventy-seven. The oldest synagogue in Greece. Go in; it is open until three, six euros, and the museum is in the old women's prayer rooms beside it. This track is quieter than the others, and it ends in silence. Let it.

Jews have lived on Rhodes for more than two thousand years. In fifteen twenty-three, the year the Knights left, the Ottomans resettled a hundred and fifty Jewish families from Salonica in this quarter, and for four centuries this was the Juderia: a Sephardic community, descended from the Jews expelled from Spain, speaking Ladino, the old Spanish of their grandparents, in these lanes. By nineteen thirty about four thousand of the island's thirty thousand people were Jewish, and there were six synagogues here. Inside, notice the plan: the reading platform in the centre, the Sephardic way, and, unusually, two Torah arks. This is the only one of the quarter's synagogues to survive the Allied bombing of nineteen forty-four.

Then the story turns. Italy's racial laws of nineteen thirty-eight drove more than two thousand people to emigrate. In September nineteen forty-three the Germans took the island from the Italians. On the eighteenth of July nineteen forty-four the German command ordered every Jewish male over sixteen to report the next morning to the Air Force headquarters with his papers. The women and children followed with their valuables. On the twenty-third of July, one thousand six hundred and seventy-three people were marched from the square just ahead of you to the harbour you landed in this morning, and packed into three boats. About a hundred Jews from the island of Kos were added on the way. Seven died in the eight-day crossing to Piraeus. From there they were sent by rail, and reached Auschwitz on the sixteenth of August nineteen forty-four. About a hundred and fifty came back.

One man in Rhodes said no. Selahattin Ülkümen, the Turkish consul, twenty-nine years old, went to the German general and argued that under Turkish law all citizens are equal, and stretched his consular protection over people with lapsed papers and over the spouses of Turkish citizens. He saved between forty and fifty people. His wife was fatally injured when the consulate was bombed. In nineteen eighty-nine Israel named him Righteous Among the Nations.

When you come out, walk to the square. It is called the Square of the Jewish Martyrs. The bronze seahorses on the fountain are the square's older, gentler landmark. The black six-sided memorial, dedicated in two thousand and two, speaks in six languages: English, French, Greek, Hebrew, Italian, and Ladino.

About forty Jews live on Rhodes today. Survivor Samuel Modiano said of that month: instead of killing us on the spot, on our island, we were transported to the camps and murdered in secret. …

The track ends here. When you are ready, lunch is three minutes away, on a quiet street where the noise of the bazaar stops.
